study.title: Resting-State fMRI Reveals the Neural Correlates of Acupuncture in the Treatment of Vascular Cognitive Impairment
study.study_design: narrative review / synthesis of existing rs-fMRI and acupuncture literature for VCI
study.population: Patients with vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) and related cognitive disorders; also includes healthy volunteers and other neurological/neurodegenerative populations discussed in cited studies
study.disease_condition: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI), including mild cognitive impairment (MCI), vascular dementia, and related cerebrovascular cognitive disorders

arms.arm_label_exact: VCI patients (observational/control group in rs-fMRI studies)

interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: Acupuncture exerts its therapeutic effects by amplifying localized stimuli through specific acupoints, which are then transmitted via the body's meridian system to regulate systemic networks.

interventions.procedure_label_exact: Acupuncture Stimulation of Hegu (LI4) and Taichong (LR3)

sensory_interoceptive_responses.notes: The paper mentions Deqi in the context of BL40 stimulation (rs-fMRI study of Deqi via acupuncturing stimulation at BL40 by rs-fMRI), but no quantitative deqi data are reported in this review paper itself.

neuroimaging_methods.motion_exclusion_exact: Head motion artifacts during scanning notably confound FC measurements by introducing spatiotemporal noise and reducing signal quality.

extraction_notes.note: This is a narrative review paper, not a primary study. No original participant data, coordinates, or quantitative neuroimaging results are reported from a single study. All neuroimaging results are drawn from cited primary studies and reported narratively or in summary tables (Tables 1 and 2). No original MRI acquisition parameters are provided.
No quantitative sensory or deqi measurements are reported in this review. The paper mentions Deqi in the context of a cited rs-fMRI study at BL40, but provides no numeric data.

Expectancy, credibility, blinding, and allocation guessing measures are not reported or assessed in this review. The limitations section notes that studies frequently fail to document subjects' prior acupuncture exposure.
No sham acupuncture arm or sham procedure details are described in this review. One limitation noted is the lack of a sham acupuncture control group in the referenced RCT (Lin et al, ref 89).

Table 1 presents summarized key findings from multiple different primary studies, not from a single study. It is not possible to link each finding to a specific sample size, threshold, or statistical result without consulting the referenced primary papers.

Table 2 presents results from multiple distinct fMRI studies of VCI. Each row represents a separate study with its own methods, sample size, and outcomes. These have been extracted separately in the neural_results contrasts and clinical_behavioral_outcomes sections where possible.
No MNI/Talairach coordinates are reported anywhere in this review paper. All neuroimaging results are narrative or cluster-level regional descriptions without spatial coordinates.
Specific acupoints for most VCI acupuncture treatment protocols referenced in this paper are not listed in the review text, except for GB34, KI3, BL40, LI4, and LR3 in specific cited studies.

The paper references a randomized controlled multicenter trial (ref 9 in references, citing Yang et al 2025) demonstrating superior ADAS-Cog reductions with acupuncture vs pharmacotherapy. However, the detailed methods, sample sizes per arm, and quantitative results are not reproduced in this review.
The sample size of 140 extracted for the Lin et al RCT (ref 89, Table 2) applies to that cited study. The review paper itself has no enrolled or analyzed sample.
Coordinate space (MNI vs Talairach) is not reported for any cited neuroimaging findings. All coordinate_space_reported_exact values have been set to 'not_reported'.
Statistical thresholds, correction methods, and exact p-values for neuroimaging contrasts described in the text are not provided in this review for the cited primary studies.

The review conflates multiple heterogeneous populations (VCI, MCI, AD, post-stroke, healthy controls) across different cited studies when discussing rs-fMRI findings. Each contrast extracted has been attributed to the most specific population described in the corresponding text passage.
